      Dominion Dynamics, Telesat team up on Arctic defence project

      By David Sali
      November 19, 2026

        One of Ottawa’s fastest-growing defence startups is teaming up with Telesat to develop a multimillion-dollar system to help soldiers communicate in the Far North. Dominion Dynamics announced Thursday it was partnering with a subsidiary of the Ottawa-based satellite services provider to create antennas and miniature terminals small enough to fit in a soldier’s backpack and rugged enough to withstand harsh environments such as the Arctic. The antennas would securely connect troops and unmanned vehicles to a network of low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites that Telesat is preparing to launch next year, the companies said in a news release Thursday.  They said the system is “intended to provide operators in the Arctic with a Canadian-controlled communications link to command centres across the country.” The first phase of the program has a price tag of about $2.2 million, the companies said in the release. Dominion and Telesat will split most of the costs, with the National Research Council of Canada contributing to Dominion’s share through its Industrial Research Assistance Program. Dominion Dynamics, which was founded in June 2025, is best known for AuraNet, a network of sensors and a map-based platform that can collect, trace and transmit information from remote regions with no or patchy cell service. The company is also developing an uncrewed, AI-powered drone called Scout that is designed to operate independently or alongside fighter jets. It will be deployable to environments too dangerous or remote to risk sending pilots into. Dominion chief operating officer Mitch Carkner said the partnership will help ensure that military personnel and equipment can communicate with each other on a secure, sovereign platform. “Our focus is creating command-and-control (technology) and connectivity across Canada through our AuraNet platform, and you can only do so much of that using radio-mesh (wireless) networks on the ground,” he explained in an interview.  “You need to have satellite back-haul to create a five-gig pipe or a 10-gig pipe. Knowing that Lightspeed is coming online (and) it’s Canadian controlled, we were really focusing on working together.”

        'A natural partnership'

        Telesat already operates ground stations in the North, but “those obviously do not work for an individual soldier or for autonomous assets — ground vehicles, drones or large drones like our Scout,” he added. The company wants to build a satellite antenna, terminal and battery pack small enough to fit into a standard military backpack and light enough for a soldier to haul around. But that’s easier said than done, Carkner noted. “If you go and talk to any soldier and say, ‘Hey, I want to put a 40-pound thing in your backpack,’ they’re going to tell you to jump off a cliff. It’s all about weight, power and managing the environment with the strongest connection possible to a satellite system.”  Stephen Hampton, vice-president, Canada and Sovereign Initiatives at Telesat, said his firm has been looking for ways to tap into the Kanata startup’s expertise for months.   “It was really kind of a natural partnership with Dominion,” he told OBJ on Thursday. “We’ve been really pleased with it, and we’re excited to roll up our sleeves and get to work.” Dominion hopes to have five to seven prototypes ready to connect with Lightspeed next year to test the technology and give Telesat’s LEO constellation a dry run before it goes into commercial service, which is expected to happen in the first quarter of 2028. Dominion’s long-term goal is to equip every Canadian soldier in the Arctic with the portable antenna system, Carkner said. But the technology could have broader applications as well.  Noting that high-speed networks are spotty in many northern communities, Carkner said Dominion’s system could make wireless communication in the region more reliable. While the program will initially be tailored to the Canadian Armed Forces, Carkner said later phases will be “more commercially focused.” “While the CAF are the first intended users, the same technology could also serve the Canadian Rangers, the Canadian Coast Guard, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and emergency management in the High North,” he added in the news release Thursday. Dominion is leading the project as the prime contractor, with Telesat LEO acting as the subcontractor. It’s the latest win for the Kanata-based defence startup, which has raised nearly $170 million in venture capital in its first 18 months and expects to employ nearly 200 people by the end of the year. Carkner said the pairing of two of Ottawa’s most prominent tech enterprises is a sign of things to come for the city’s growing defence industry ecosystem.  “Players that have been in the game for a while are looking to other companies to drive innovation,” he said. “I think it’s a great sign for other founders and entrepreneurs in the city that you can start a company, you can go work with a great business like Telesat and solve big problems.” Hampton said the partnership could pave the way for future collaborations between the two firms.  “You’ve got two highly motivated, ambitious companies that are investing and innovating and developing next-generation technologies for our members in uniform,” Hampton said. “There definitely could be more opportunities down the road.”
